young.html: Shakespeare wrote ten plays about the kings of England who lived one to two hundred years before him. They are full of crowns, battles, plots and speeches. Together they tell how England's kings lost the crown, fought for it, and finally made peace.

The most famous young hero is Prince Hal. He spends his days in a tavern with a fat, funny, boastful knight named Sir John Falstaff, and everyone thinks Hal will be a terrible king. But when he becomes King Henry V, he leads a small, tired English army to victory at the Battle of Agincourt.

Or close the wall up with our English dead.

young.html: Rally the team. Before battle, Henry V gives speeches to cheer his soldiers. Write a short speech to cheer up a team before a big game or a hard test. Use "we" a lot, and end with a line people will remember.

full.html: In the 1590s Shakespeare wrote two linked groups of four plays. The first, written first, covers the later story: the three parts of Henry VI and Richard III, from the loss of France through the Wars of the Roses to the Battle of Bosworth (1485). The second, often called the Henriad, goes back to the beginning: Richard II, Henry IV Parts 1 and 2, and Henry V. He also wrote King John and, near the end of his career, Henry VIII with John Fletcher.

full.cap: Reigns by royal house. The shaded band marks the Wars of the Roses.

full.html: His main source was Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles (1587). He compressed years into scenes, invented speeches and characters (Falstaff above all), and shaped history into drama. His audience lived under Elizabeth I, granddaughter of Henry VII, the Tudor who won at Bosworth, so the plays' ending in Tudor peace mattered to them.

Richard II believes a king rules by God's right and cannot be touched. His cousin Henry Bolingbroke, whom he has exiled and robbed, comes back with an army and takes the throne as Henry IV. Before that, the dying John of Gaunt mourns what England has become.

full.html: Henry IV's reign is troubled by rebellion and by guilt over how he took the crown. His son Hal seems to waste his youth with Falstaff, a witty, cowardly, lovable old knight. Hal tells the audience early on that he is biding his time. He proves himself at the Battle of Shrewsbury, and when he becomes king he publicly rejects Falstaff. Readers have argued ever since whether that is wise statesmanship or a cold betrayal of a friend.

full.html: The Chorus asks the audience to imagine armies and oceans on a small wooden stage. Henry invades France and, at Agincourt in 1415, defeats a much larger army. The play celebrates him, yet it also shows the cost of war: hanged friends, frightened soldiers, and a king who wonders, alone at night, what he owes the men who die for him.

At the far end of the story, Richard of Gloucester schemes and kills his way to the throne, letting the audience in on every plan. He is defeated at Bosworth by Henry Tudor. Historians have long debated how much of this dark portrait is fair, since it came from Tudor writers with reasons to blacken him.
Treating the plays as accurate history. They are dramas based on chronicles, written to move and entertain. They are best read alongside a good history of the period.

deep.html: The history plays keep asking: is a king made by birth, by God, by ability, or by the consent of the people? Richard II has the right but not the skill; Henry IV has the skill but not the right; Henry V seems to have both, yet the plays show what his greatness costs. Machiavelli's The Prince, earlier in this era, asks the same questions in prose.

items: Is it ever right to remove a bad ruler by force?
Was Hal right to reject Falstaff? What does a leader owe old friends?
Can a play about war celebrate courage without celebrating war?

questions: Prince Hal surprises everyone by becoming a great king. Have you ever been underestimated?
Henry V calls his soldiers "dear friends." What makes people willing to follow a leader?
Was it fair of Henry V to turn his back on Falstaff?
Why might a playwright change history to tell a better story? Is that all right?
care: The history plays include battles, executions and political murders. This lesson summarizes them without detail.
